evidence.reference_title: Genetic variation in the human androgen receptor gene is the major determinant of common early-onset androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: The investigation of a large number of genetic variants covering the AR locus suggests that a polyglycine-encoding GGN repeat in exon 1 is a plausible candidate for conferring the functional effect.

evidence.reference_title: Polymorphism of the androgen receptor gene is associated with male pattern baldness.
evidence.snippet: The androgen receptor gene StuI restriction site was found in all but one (98.1%) of the 54 young bald men (p = 0.0005) and in 92.3% of older balding men (p = 0.000004) but in only 76.6% of nonbald men.

evidence.reference_title: EDA2R is associated with androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: We found that the non-synonymous SNP rs1385699 on EDA2R gave the best result (P=3.9e(-19)) whereas rs6152 on the AR gene is less significant (P=4.17e(-12)).

nodes.description: The hair cycle of an affected follicle is re-proportioned: anagen shortens with each cycle, catagen arrives early, and telogen and the empty kenogen interval between shedding and regrowth lengthen, so a growing proportion of follicles are resting or empty at any moment and the hair that does grow has less time to lengthen. Interleukin-6 and prostaglandin D2 both promote regression directly. Minoxidil acts here, shortening telogen and prolonging anagen, which is how a drug with no effect on androgen metabolism regrows hair.
nodes.id: Anagen Shortening and Premature Catagen Entry

evidence.reference_title: Risk factors for androgenetic alopecia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
evidence.snippet: Androgenetic alopecia (AGA), the most prevalent type of hair loss, is characterized by progressive hair follicle miniaturization and disruption of the hair growth cycle, with a shortened anagen phase and an extended telogen phase, eventually leading to baldness [1].

evidence.reference_title: Trichoscopy of Androgenetic Alopecia: A Systematic Review.
evidence.snippet: The reduction in hair density may also be attributed to the extension of the kenogen phase, occurring concurrently with the miniaturization process of the hair follicle in the frontoparietal region [4].

evidence.reference_title: Dihydrotestosterone-inducible IL-6 inhibits elongation of human hair shafts by suppressing matrix cell proliferation and promotes regression of hair follicles in mice.
evidence.snippet: Recombinant human IL-6 (rhIL-6) inhibited hair shaft elongation and suppressed proliferation of matrix cells in cultured human hair follicles.

evidence.reference_title: Prostaglandin D2 inhibits hair growth and is elevated in bald scalp of men with androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: During normal follicle cycling in mice, Ptgds and PGD(2) levels increase immediately preceding the regression phase, suggesting an inhibitory effect on hair growth.

nodes.description: What the dermal papilla secretes changes under dihydrotestosterone. Three inhibitors are established in balding dermal papilla cells: transforming growth factor beta-1, induced by androgen and neutralized by antibody to reverse the growth inhibition of co-cultured keratinocytes; dickkopf-1, among the most upregulated genes within hours of dihydrotestosterone, secreted, and elevated in bald over haired scalp; and interleukin-6, induced within hours, secreted, and acting on receptor-bearing matrix keratinocytes. Balding dermal papilla cells also under-express vasculature-related genes. In beard dermal papilla the same androgen induces growth factors including insulin-like growth factor 1, so the identity of the secreted factors, not the hormone, sets the direction of the response.
nodes.id: Androgen-Driven Paracrine Inhibitory Output from the Dermal Papilla

cell_types: scalp hair follicle dermal papilla cell

evidence.reference_title: Androgen-inducible TGF-beta1 from balding dermal papilla cells inhibits epithelial cell growth: a clue to understand paradoxical effects of androgen on human hair growth.
evidence.snippet: Moreover, the neutralizing anti-TGF-beta1 antibody reversed the androgen-elicited growth inhibition of KCs in a dose-dependent manner.

evidence.reference_title: Role of androgen in mesenchymal epithelial interactions in human hair follicle.
evidence.snippet: This growth suppression of KC was mediated by transforming growth factor-beta1 (TGF-beta1) derived from DPC of AGA, suggesting that TGF-beta1 is a paracrine mediator for AGA.

evidence.reference_title: Dihydrotestosterone-inducible dickkopf 1 from balding dermal papilla cells causes apoptosis in follicular keratinocytes.
evidence.snippet: DKK-1 messenger RNA is upregulated in 3-6 hours after 50-100 nM DHT treatment and ELISA showed that DKK-1 is secreted from DP cells in response to DHT.

evidence.reference_title: Dihydrotestosterone-inducible dickkopf 1 from balding dermal papilla cells causes apoptosis in follicular keratinocytes.
evidence.snippet: Moreover, immunoblotting showed that the DKK-1 level is up in the bald scalp compared with the haired scalp of patients with androgenetic alopecia.

evidence.reference_title: Dihydrotestosterone-inducible IL-6 inhibits elongation of human hair shafts by suppressing matrix cell proliferation and promotes regression of hair follicles in mice.
evidence.snippet: IL-6 was upregulated 3 hours after 10-100 nM DHT treatment, and ELISA showed that IL-6 was secreted from balding DP cells in response to DHT.

evidence.reference_title: Differential Expression between Human Dermal Papilla Cells from Balding and Non-Balding Scalps Reveals New Candidate Genes for Androgenetic Alopecia.
evidence.snippet: Down-regulated genes in BAB compared to BAN were highly enriched for vasculature-related genes, suggesting that deficiency of DPC from balding scalps in fostering vascularization around the hair follicle may contribute to the development of AGA.

evidence.reference_title: Role of androgen in mesenchymal epithelial interactions in human hair follicle.
evidence.snippet: Insulin-like growth factor-I was identified as one of the androgen-dependent paracrine growth factors produced by beard DPC.

nodes.description: Testosterone is reduced to the more potent dihydrotestosterone by 5-alpha-reductase within the follicle, type 2 being the isoform expressed in frontal scalp dermal papilla. The balding scalp carries high levels of dihydrotestosterone. The requirement is proven at both ends: men with inherited 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, and eunuchs, do not bald, and blocking the enzyme with finasteride lowers scalp dihydrotestosterone and regrows hair. Circulating androgen is not the variable; men with pattern hair loss have normal serum testosterone, and the disease is a property of local conversion and local sensitivity.
nodes.id: Conversion of Testosterone to Dihydrotestosterone in the Dermal Papilla

evidence.reference_title: Molecular mechanisms of androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: Conversion of testosterone to DHT within the dermal papilla plays a central role, while androgen-regulated factors deriving from dermal papilla cells are believed to influence growth of other components of the hair follicle.

evidence.reference_title: Androgens and alopecia.
evidence.snippet: Observations in both eunuchs, who have low levels of testicular androgens, and males with genetic 5alpha-reductase (5alphaR) deficiency, who have low levels of dihydrotestosterone (DHT), implicate DHT as a key androgen in the pathogenesis of MPHL in men.

evidence.reference_title: Polymorphism of the androgen receptor gene is associated with male pattern baldness.
evidence.snippet: A balding scalp is characterized by high levels of the potent androgen dihydrotestosterone and increased expression of the androgen receptor gene.

evidence.reference_title: Role of androgen in mesenchymal epithelial interactions in human hair follicle.
evidence.snippet: These DPC show strong expression of androgen receptors, and the expression of type II 5alpha reductase is restricted to beard and frontal scalp DPC.

nodes.description: The female pattern: widening of the central part and diffuse thinning over the crown, frontal and parietal scalp with the frontal hairline kept, graded on the Ludwig scale. A male-type pattern occurs exceptionally in women.
nodes.id: Diffuse central scalp thinning with preserved frontal hairline

evidence.reference_title: Trichoscopy of Androgenetic Alopecia: A Systematic Review.
evidence.snippet: In female androgenetic alopecia (FAGA), hair thinning occurs over the frontal and parietal areas of the scalp (Ludwig type)

evidence.reference_title: Classification of the types of androgenetic alopecia (common baldness) occurring in the female sex.
evidence.snippet: The exceptionally observed male type of androgenetic alopecia can be classified according to Hamilton or to the modification of this classification proposed by Ebling & Rook.

nodes.description: The dermal papilla, not the follicular epithelium, is the androgen target. Androgen receptor is confined to dermal papilla cells, and in co-culture testosterone changes the growth of outer root sheath keratinocytes only when dermal papilla cells from an androgen-responsive site are present, without cell contact, so the receptor's effect on the epithelium must be relayed by secreted factors. In balding scalp dermal papilla cells transfected to restore androgen receptor, androgen suppresses keratinocyte growth by about half; in beard dermal papilla the same receptor drives growth, which is the paradox of androgens on human hair and the reason this node is about the responding cell rather than the hormone. The receptor blocker RU 58841 abolishes the inhibitory effect in macaque co-culture, and antiandrogens are the basis of treatment in women.
nodes.id: Dihydrotestosterone-Androgen Receptor Signalling in Dermal Papilla Cells

cell_types: scalp hair follicle dermal papilla cell

evidence.reference_title: Interaction between dermal papilla cells and follicular epithelial cells in vitro: effect of androgen.
evidence.snippet: Epithelial cells of the hair follicles were not stained by the antibody.

evidence.reference_title: Androgen-inducible TGF-beta1 from balding dermal papilla cells inhibits epithelial cell growth: a clue to understand paradoxical effects of androgen on human hair growth.
evidence.snippet: In this modified coculture, androgen significantly suppressed the growth of KCs by approximately 50%, indicating that overexpression of AR can restore the responsiveness of the DPCs to androgen in vivo.

evidence.reference_title: Inhibition of hair growth by testosterone in the presence of dermal papilla cells from the frontal bald scalp of the postpubertal stumptailed macaque.
evidence.snippet: Furthermore, RU 58841, an androgen receptor blocker, antagonized this testosterone-elicited inhibition.

evidence.reference_title: Premature senescence of balding dermal papilla cells in vitro is associated with p16(INK4a) expression.
evidence.snippet: In AGA, it has been proposed that the inhibitory actions of androgens are mediated via the DP although the molecular nature of these interactions is poorly understood.

nodes.description: Oral dutasteride inhibits both type 1 and type 2 5-alpha-reductase. In a randomized placebo-controlled trial of 416 men it increased target-area hair counts dose-dependently and at 2.5 mg was superior to finasteride 5 mg at 12 and 24 weeks, with scalp and serum dihydrotestosterone falling in step. Approved for pattern hair loss in Japan and South Korea and used off-label elsewhere at 0.5 mg; the adverse-effect profile is that of finasteride with the same concern about sexual and mood effects.
nodes.id: Dutasteride

evidence.reference_title: The importance of dual 5alpha-reductase inhibition in the treatment of male pattern hair loss: results of a randomized placebo-controlled study of dutasteride versus finasteride.
evidence.snippet: Dutasteride increased target area hair count versus placebo in a dose-dependent fashion and dutasteride 2.5 mg was superior to finasteride at 12 and 24 weeks.

nodes.id: EDA2R

evidence.reference_title: EDA2R is associated with androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: In particular, we found that rs1352015 located 8 kb from the EDA2R gene showed the best result (P=7.77e(-7)).

evidence.reference_title: Differential Expression between Human Dermal Papilla Cells from Balding and Non-Balding Scalps Reveals New Candidate Genes for Androgenetic Alopecia.
evidence.snippet: We found evidence for AR but not EDA2R as the candidate gene at the AGA risk locus on chromosome X.

nodes.description: Oral finasteride 1 mg daily, a competitive inhibitor of type 2 5-alpha-reductase, lowers serum and scalp dihydrotestosterone and in two one-year trials of 1,553 men slowed hair loss and increased hair counts by 107 hairs at one year and 138 at two against placebo, with progressive loss on placebo. Histology shows a trend to reversal of miniaturization. It is the therapy that proves the mechanism. It is approved for men only; it did not help postmenopausal women with the female pattern in a controlled trial, and it is contraindicated in pregnancy. Sexual adverse effects occur in a small minority and persistent sexual and mood symptoms are the subject of regulatory warnings.
nodes.id: Finasteride

evidence.reference_title: Finasteride in the treatment of men with androgenetic alopecia. Finasteride Male Pattern Hair Loss Study Group.
evidence.snippet: In men with male pattern hair loss, finasteride 1 mg/d slowed the progression of hair loss and increased hair growth in clinical trials over 2 years.

evidence.reference_title: Finasteride in the treatment of men with androgenetic alopecia. Finasteride Male Pattern Hair Loss Study Group.
evidence.snippet: Clinically significant increases in hair count (baseline = 876 hairs), measured in a 1-inch diameter circular area (5.1 cm2) of balding vertex scalp, were observed with finasteride treatment (107 and 138 hairs vs placebo at 1 and 2 years, respectively; P < .001).

evidence.reference_title: Androgens and alopecia.
evidence.snippet: In contrast to its beneficial effects in men, finasteride did not improve hair growth in postmenopausal women with FPHL.

nodes.description: The product of a miniaturized follicle: short, fine, often less pigmented hairs replacing terminal hairs in the affected regions. Seen on trichoscopy as vellus hairs in about two thirds of patients and on biopsy as a reduced terminal-to-vellus ratio.
nodes.id: Fine, short vellus-like scalp hairs

evidence.reference_title: Possible mechanisms of miniaturization during androgenetic alopecia or pattern hair loss.
evidence.snippet: In androgenetic alopecia, or pattern hair loss, follicles undergo miniaturization, shrinking from terminal to vellus-like hairs.

evidence.reference_title: Trichoscopy of Androgenetic Alopecia: A Systematic Review.
evidence.snippet: The most common features identified using trichoscopy included hair diameter variability (94.07% of patients), vellus hairs (66.45%) and the peripilar sign (43.27%).

nodes.description: The male pattern: bitemporal recession of the frontal hairline and a thinning vertex that enlarge and merge, graded on the Hamilton-Norwood scale toward a retained occipital and parietal horseshoe. About one man in eight has a predominantly frontal variant.
nodes.id: Frontotemporal hairline recession and vertex thinning

evidence.reference_title: Trichoscopy of Androgenetic Alopecia: A Systematic Review.
evidence.snippet: Typically, hair thinning in the frontotemporal areas, the recession of the frontotemporal hairline and hair loss in the vertex area occur in male androgenetic alopecia (MAGA).

evidence.reference_title: Dissection of genetic variation and evidence for pleiotropy in male pattern baldness.
evidence.snippet: The balding process is highly patterned, suggesting that MPB progression is induced by some ageing-associated program: from initial frontotemporal hairline recession to a more severe occipital horseshoe stage1.

evidence.reference_title: Prevalence of male pattern hair loss in 18-49 year old men.
evidence.snippet: Twelve percent of the men were classified as having predominantly frontal baldness (type A variants).

nodes.description: Shafts of visibly different calibre side by side, conventionally more than 20 percent of hairs differing, because follicles miniaturize asynchronously. The most consistent trichoscopic sign, present in about 94 percent of patients, and the sign that makes trichoscopy the confirmatory test in women, where the clinical picture is less specific. Accompanied by the peripilar sign in about 43 percent. No HPO term describes this dermoscopic finding, so it is left unbound.
nodes.id: Hair diameter variability on trichoscopy

evidence.reference_title: Trichoscopy of Androgenetic Alopecia: A Systematic Review.
evidence.snippet: The most common features identified using trichoscopy included hair diameter variability (94.07% of patients), vellus hairs (66.45%) and the peripilar sign (43.27%).

evidence.reference_title: Trichoscopy of Androgenetic Alopecia: A Systematic Review.
evidence.snippet: In the majority of male androgenetic alopecia cases, a patient's history and clinical evaluation may be sufficient to establish the diagnosis, while for women, they should be supplemented with trichoscopy.

nodes.description: Surgical redistribution of follicular units from the androgen-insensitive occipital and parietal donor scalp to the balding recipient area, either by strip harvest with stereomicroscopic dissection or by follicular unit extraction through 1 mm punches, which avoids a linear donor scar. It is the only durable structural treatment and works because transplanted follicles keep the androgen response of their donor site. Donor supply is finite, so it is reserved for stable, sufficiently advanced disease, and medical treatment continues to protect the non-transplanted hair.
nodes.id: Hair transplantation (follicular unit transplantation or extraction)

evidence.reference_title: Follicular unit transplantation: 2005.
evidence.snippet: The recognition that the follicular unit is a discrete, anatomic and physiologic entity, and that preserving it through stereomicroscopic dissection is the best way to ensure the naturalness of the restoration, has brought hair transplantation into the twenty-first century.

evidence.reference_title: Follicular unit transplantation: 2005.
evidence.snippet: The essence of providing the best care for patients rests on proper patient selection, establishing realistic expectations, and using nonsurgical management for young persons who are just starting to thin.

evidence.reference_title: Follicular unit extraction: minimally invasive surgery for hair transplantation.
evidence.snippet: FUE is a minimally invasive approach to hair transplantation that obviates the need for a linear donor incision.

nodes.description: A mouse expressing prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 2 under the keratin 14 promoter, which raises skin prostaglandin D2 and develops alopecia, follicular miniaturization and sebaceous gland hyperplasia. It models the prostaglandin arm in isolation: there is no androgen drive, no susceptibility genetics and no scalp pattern, so it speaks to what prostaglandin D2 can do to a follicle, not to how the human disease arises.
nodes.id: K14-Ptgs2 transgenic mouse (skin-targeted prostaglandin overproduction)

evidence.reference_title: Prostaglandin D2 inhibits hair growth and is elevated in bald scalp of men with androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: These results define PGD(2) as an inhibitor of hair growth in AGA and suggest the PGD(2)-GPR44 pathway as a potential target for treatment.

nodes.description: Home-use laser combs and helmets cleared as devices. In four randomized, sham-controlled, double-blind trials of 269 men and women, 26 weeks of treatment three times a week increased terminal hair density by about 18 to 26 hairs per square centimetre over sham, with no serious adverse events. The effect is modest, the mechanism in the follicle is not established, and the link into the pathograph is therefore recorded as modulation of the miniaturization node rather than as a specific action.
nodes.id: Low-level laser therapy (photobiomodulation)

evidence.reference_title: Efficacy and safety of a low-level laser device in the treatment of male and female pattern hair loss: a multicenter, randomized, sham device-controlled, double-blind study.
evidence.snippet: Randomized, sham device-controlled, double-blind clinical trials were conducted at multiple institutional and private practices.

nodes.description: Weekly scalp microneedling with a dermaroller added to twice-daily 5 percent topical minoxidil. In a randomized, evaluator-blinded pilot study of 100 men with Norwood III vertex or IV disease, the combination gave a mean 12-week hair-count gain of 91.4 against 22.2 per square centimetre for minoxidil alone, with 82 percent of combination patients reporting more than 50 percent improvement against 4.5 percent, and patients who had not responded to conventional therapy responded. The proposed rationale is wound-induced activation of growth factors and Wnt signalling in the dermal papilla and its associated stem cells, which is stated, not measured, in the trial. A single unreplicated pilot, so the evidence is weaker than for the licensed drugs. NCIT has no clinical-action term for microneedling (its microneedle terms are drug-delivery devices), so the generic Therapeutic Procedure term is bound and the specificity is carried in the preferred term.
nodes.id: Microneedling adjunct to topical minoxidil

evidence.reference_title: A randomized evaluator blinded study of effect of microneedling in androgenetic alopecia: a pilot study.
evidence.snippet: After randomization one group was offered weekly microneedling treatment with twice daily 5% minoxidil lotion (Microneedling group); other group was given only 5% minoxidil lotion.

evidence.reference_title: A randomized evaluator blinded study of effect of microneedling in androgenetic alopecia: a pilot study.
evidence.snippet: The mean change in hair count at week 12 was significantly greater for the Microneedling group compared to the Minoxidil group (91.4 vs 22.2 respectively).

evidence.reference_title: A randomized evaluator blinded study of effect of microneedling in androgenetic alopecia: a pilot study.
evidence.snippet: In the Microneedling group, 41 (82%) patients reported more than 50% improvement versus only 2 (4.5%) patients in the Minoxidil group. Unsatisfied patients to conventional therapy for AGA got good response with Microneedling treatment.

nodes.description: Topical minoxidil 2 to 5 percent is approved for either sex; 5 percent solution gave 45 percent more regrowth than 2 percent at 48 weeks in men and improved psychosocial perceptions, at the cost of more irritation. It acts on the hair cycle rather than on androgen metabolism, shortening telogen and prolonging anagen, and its follicular target is not settled; the sulphated metabolite opens KATP channels and stimulates vascular endothelial growth factor and prostaglandin synthesis in vitro. Response requires continuous use and is preceded by transient shedding. Low-dose oral minoxidil (about 0.25 to 5 mg daily) is used off-label where topical therapy is not tolerated; across 17 studies it was effective and well tolerated in healthy patients, with hypertrichosis, oedema and cardiovascular effects the concerns needing screening. Randomized phase III trials of the oral route are now registered in women (1 mg against topical 2 percent and placebo) and in men (titrated to at most 5 mg against placebo); see clinical_trials.
nodes.id: Minoxidil (topical; low-dose oral off-label)

evidence.reference_title: A randomized clinical trial of 5% topical minoxidil versus 2% topical minoxidil and placebo in the treatment of androgenetic alopecia in men.
evidence.snippet: In men with AGA, 5% topical minoxidil was clearly superior to 2% topical minoxidil and placebo in increasing hair regrowth, and the magnitude of its effect was marked (45% more hair regrowth than 2% topical minoxidil at week 48).

evidence.reference_title: Oral minoxidil treatment for hair loss: A review of efficacy and safety.
evidence.snippet: Oral minoxidil was found to be an effective and well-tolerated treatment alternative for healthy patients having difficulty with topical formulations.

evidence.reference_title: International Phase III, Multi Center, Randomized, Double Blind, Placebo and Active Controlled and Parallel Group Clinical Trial to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of Oral Minoxidil 1 mg in Female Patients With Androgenetic Alopecia
evidence.snippet: The goal of this clinical trial is to learn about oral minoxidil 1mg in the treatment of women with androgenetic alopecia, a type of hormone-imbalanced hair loss.

evidence.reference_title: A Phase 3, Prospective, Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Parallel-Group, Multicenter Clinical Trial to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of N1087 in Male Participants With Androgenetic Alopecia.
evidence.snippet: This study is a Phase 3 clinical trial designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of N1087 compared with placebo in adult men with androgenetic alopecia (male pattern hair loss).

evidence.reference_title: Minoxidil: mechanisms of action on hair growth.
evidence.snippet: There is some evidence that the stimulatory effect of minoxidil on hair growth is also due to the opening of potassium channels by minoxidil sulphate, but this idea has been difficult to prove and to date there has been no clear demonstration that KATP channels are expressed in the hair follicle.

nodes.description: Spironolactone 200 mg daily or cyproterone acetate is used off-label in women with the female pattern. In an open before-after series of 80 women with biopsy-confirmed miniaturization, 44 percent regrew, 44 percent were stable and 12 percent continued to lose over at least a year, with no difference between the two drugs and no prediction of response by serum hormones, ferritin, age or menopausal status. There is no placebo-controlled trial, and the authors themselves note that whether the female pattern is androgen-driven at all is not established. Reliable contraception is required.
nodes.id: Oral antiandrogens in women (spironolactone, cyproterone acetate)

evidence.reference_title: Treatment of female pattern hair loss with oral antiandrogens.
evidence.snippet: Thirty-five (44%) women had hair regrowth, 35 (44%) had no clear change in hair density before and after treatment, and 10 (12%) experienced continuing hair loss during the treatment period.

evidence.reference_title: Treatment of female pattern hair loss with oral antiandrogens.
evidence.snippet: A placebo-controlled study is required to compare this outcome to the natural history of FPHL.

nodes.description: The disease itself as a finding: progressive thinning of scalp hair in a reproducible pattern, with follicular openings preserved, beginning after puberty and advancing at a variable rate over decades. Obligate, since it is the definition.
nodes.id: Patterned non-scarring scalp hair loss

evidence.reference_title: Molecular mechanisms of androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: Androgenetic alopecia (AGA) is hereditary and androgen-dependent, progressive thinning of the scalp hair that follows a defined pattern.

evidence.reference_title: Trichoscopy of Androgenetic Alopecia: A Systematic Review.
evidence.snippet: Androgenetic alopecia (AGA), also known as pattern hair loss, is the most common cause of non-scarring alopecia.

nodes.description: In transitional and balding zones the follicular adventitial sheath thickens, mast cells degranulate and fibroblasts activate within it, and activated T cells infiltrate around the lower infundibulum and the bulge, the stem cell niche, with class II antigen induction on adventitial venules. A perifollicular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate and fibrosis are also seen in women with the female pattern, and in a subset progress to follicular drop-out and permanent loss. The finding matters clinically: patients with significant inflammation on biopsy regrow less on minoxidil (55 versus 77 percent). Whether the microinflammation is a cause, a cofactor or a consequence of miniaturization is unresolved and is recorded as a discussion.
nodes.id: Perifollicular Microinflammation and Fibrosis

evidence.reference_title: Characterization of inflammatory infiltrates in male pattern alopecia: implications for pathogenesis.
evidence.snippet: Immunohistochemically, control biopsies were devoid of follicular inflammation (n = 3), while transitional regions consistently showed the presence of activated T-cell infiltrates about the lower portions of follicular infundibula.

evidence.reference_title: Characterization of inflammatory infiltrates in male pattern alopecia: implications for pathogenesis.
evidence.snippet: This finding was associated with mast cell degranulation and fibroblast activation within the fibrous sheaths.

evidence.reference_title: Female pattern hair loss and its relationship to permanent/cicatricial alopecia: a new perspective.
evidence.snippet: The presence of a perifollicular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate and fibrosis is seen without follicular drop-out in biopsies of women with FPHL and with a notable follicular drop-out in a cicatricial form of this condition (heretofore called cicatricial pattern hair loss) as well as in fibrosing alopecia in a pattern distribution, currently classified as a subset of lichen planopilaris.

evidence.reference_title: Diagnostic and predictive value of horizontal sections of scalp biopsy specimens in male pattern androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: In MPAA with no significant inflammation, regrowth occurred in 77% of cases, versus 55% in cases with significant inflammation.

evidence.reference_title: Molecular mechanisms of androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: Since the clinical success rate of treatment of AGA with modulators of androgen metabolism or hair growth promoters is limited, sustained microscopic follicular inflammation with connective tissue remodeling, eventually resulting in permanent hair loss, is considered a possible cofactor in the complex etiology of AGA.

nodes.description: Autologous platelet-rich plasma injected into the scalp, usually three monthly sessions with maintenance every three to six months. A meta-analysis finds a moderate standardized mean difference in hair density of about 0.5 against placebo, but preparation, dosing and endpoints vary between studies and at least one double-blind split-scalp trial found no advantage over placebo. The evidence is weaker than for minoxidil, finasteride or the laser trials, and the proposed mechanism, growth-factor stimulation of follicular proliferation, is not demonstrated in patients. Bound to the generic Therapeutic Procedure term: NCIT's platelet-rich plasma terms (C106557, C177738) are substance terms outside the clinical intervention branch and the therapeutic-agent slot's chemical-entity range, so the agent is carried in the preferred_term rather than bound.
nodes.id: Platelet-rich plasma injection

evidence.reference_title: Platelet-Rich Plasma as a Treatment for Androgenetic Alopecia.
evidence.snippet: The overall SMD in hair density was 0.58 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.35-0.80) and 0.51 (95% CI: 0.23-0.80, p < .0004) in favor of PRP treatment when compared with baseline and placebo treatment, respectively.

nodes.description: The initiating lesion is inherited susceptibility, not a mutation. The strongest signal in every study is the androgen receptor / EDA2R region at Xq11-q12, where common variants including a polyglycine GGN repeat in AR exon 1 carry an etiological fraction near half of early-onset disease; a non-synonymous EDA2R variant gives the best single-marker result in a Sardinian isolate and the AR association there appears to ride on linkage disequilibrium, while expression in balding dermal papilla cells points back to AR as the functional gene. A second major locus at 20p11.22 acts independently of AR, and genome-wide meta-analyses have since added WNT10A, FGF5, IRF4, DKK2, TWIST1 and several hundred further loci, most of them regulatory and each of small effect. What any risk allele does to the follicle is not known; the one thing the genetics does say is that the predisposition is expressed in the scalp follicle's own androgen response.
nodes.id: Polygenic Susceptibility at the AR/EDA2R Locus and Autosomal Risk Loci

evidence.reference_title: Genetic variation in the human androgen receptor gene is the major determinant of common early-onset androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: We demonstrate that genetic variability in the androgen receptor gene (AR) is the cardinal prerequisite for the development of early-onset AGA, with an etiological fraction of 0.46.

evidence.reference_title: EDA2R is associated with androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: Further statistical analysis carried out by conditioning each gene to the presence of the other showed that the association with EDA2R is independent while the association with AR seems to be the result of linkage disequilibrium.

evidence.reference_title: Male-pattern baldness susceptibility locus at 20p11.
evidence.snippet: The one man in seven who harbors risk alleles at both 20p11.22 and AR (encoding the androgen receptor) has a sevenfold-increased odds of androgenic alopecia (OR = 7.12, P = 3.7 x 10(-15)).

evidence.reference_title: Susceptibility variants for male-pattern baldness on chromosome 20p11.
evidence.snippet: No interaction was detected with the X-chromosomal androgen receptor locus, suggesting that the 20p11 locus has a role in a yet-to-be-identified androgen-independent pathway.

evidence.reference_title: Meta-analysis identifies novel risk loci and yields systematic insights into the biology of male-pattern baldness.
evidence.snippet: The 63 loci explain ∼39% of the phenotypic variance in MPB and highlight several plausible candidate genes (FGF5, IRF4, DKK2) and pathways (melatonin signalling, adipogenesis) that are likely to be implicated in the key-pathophysiological features of MPB and may represent promising targets for the development of novel therapeutic options.

evidence.reference_title: Androgenetic alopecia: identification of four genetic risk loci and evidence for the contribution of WNT signaling to its etiology.
evidence.snippet: The strongest association signal was obtained for rs7349332 (P=3.55 × 10(-15)) on chr2q35, which is located intronically in WNT10A.

evidence.reference_title: Differential Expression between Human Dermal Papilla Cells from Balding and Non-Balding Scalps Reveals New Candidate Genes for Androgenetic Alopecia.
evidence.snippet: We found evidence for AR but not EDA2R as the candidate gene at the AGA risk locus on chromosome X.

evidence.reference_title: Genetic prediction of male pattern baldness.
evidence.snippet: We identified over 250 independent genetic loci associated with severe hair loss (P<5x10-8).

nodes.description: Dermal papilla cells cultured from balding scalp proliferate more slowly than those from non-balding scalp and show the morphology, beta-galactosidase staining, p16INK4a/pRb upregulation, loss of Bmi-1, and nuclear oxidative stress and DNA damage markers of premature senescence. A papilla that cannot maintain its cell number cannot maintain the size of the hair it specifies, which links this in vitro finding to the reduced dermal papilla cell number proposed to underlie miniaturization; the finding is from cultured cells and its in vivo weight is not established.
nodes.id: Premature Senescence of Balding Dermal Papilla Cells

cell_types: scalp hair follicle dermal papilla cell

evidence.reference_title: Premature senescence of balding dermal papilla cells in vitro is associated with p16(INK4a) expression.
evidence.snippet: Premature senescence of balding DPC in vitro in association with expression of p16(INK4a)/pRB suggests that balding DPC are sensitive to environmental stress and identifies alternative pathways that could lead to novel therapeutic strategies for treatment of AGA.

nodes.description: The histological hallmark. Terminal follicles convert to vellus-like follicles producing short, fine, often depigmented hairs, leaving behind fibrous streamers (stelae) below the shrunken bulb; horizontal sections show fewer terminal and more vellus hairs and a terminal-to-vellus ratio that falls from about 7:1 in normal scalp to below 4:1. Miniaturization is probably an abrupt, large-step event rather than a slow arithmetic of shortening cycles, because it can reverse within a single cycle on finasteride, and it is proposed to follow directly from a reduction in dermal papilla cell number and therefore papilla size. Follicular ostia are retained, so the process is non-scarring and, early, reversible.
nodes.id: Progressive Follicular Miniaturization with Dermal Papilla Shrinkage

animal_models.description: Frontal follicles regress with age and the regression reverses under 5-alpha-reductase inhibition, measured as hair weight and follicle length.
animal_models.name: Stump-tailed macaque spontaneous androgen-dependent frontal balding

animal_models.description: Produces follicular miniaturization and alopecia downstream of prostaglandin D2 alone.
animal_models.name: K14-Ptgs2 transgenic mouse (skin-targeted prostaglandin overproduction)

biological_processes: hair follicle maturation to a terminal follicle
cell_types: scalp hair follicle dermal papilla cell

evidence.reference_title: Androgenetic alopecia: a review.
evidence.snippet: Androgenetic alopecia is characterized by progressive hair follicular miniaturization, caused by the actions of androgens on the epithelial cells of genetically susceptible hair follicles in androgen-dependent areas.

evidence.reference_title: Possible mechanisms of miniaturization during androgenetic alopecia or pattern hair loss.
evidence.snippet: It is hypothesized that the miniaturization seen with pattern hair loss may be the direct result of reduction in the cell number and, hence, size of the dermal papilla.

evidence.reference_title: Possible mechanisms of miniaturization during androgenetic alopecia or pattern hair loss.
evidence.snippet: Evidence is presented to support a new concept that miniaturization is an abrupt, large-step process that also can be reversed in 1 hair cycle, as has been shown clinically, with confirmatory histologic evidence, in patients with pattern hair loss responding to finasteride treatment.

evidence.reference_title: Diagnostic and predictive value of horizontal sections of scalp biopsy specimens in male pattern androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of MPAA was confirmed by finding decreased terminal hairs and increased stelae and vellus hairs.

evidence.reference_title: Bald scalp in men with androgenetic alopecia retains hair follicle stem cells but lacks CD200-rich and CD34-positive hair follicle progenitor cells.
evidence.snippet: Androgenetic alopecia (AGA), also known as common baldness, is characterized by a marked decrease in hair follicle size, which could be related to the loss of hair follicle stem or progenitor cells.

nodes.description: Prostaglandin D2 synthase mRNA and protein, and prostaglandin D2 itself, are elevated in bald compared with haired scalp of the same men. Prostaglandin D2 inhibits hair growth in explanted human follicles and on mouse skin through the GPR44 (DP2/CRTH2) receptor and not through PTGDR, and in the normal mouse cycle its levels rise just before regression. A mouse over-expressing prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 2 in skin develops alopecia, miniaturization and sebaceous hyperplasia. This is the one arm of the mechanism with a defined drug-able receptor; its relation to the androgen arm is unresolved.
nodes.id: Prostaglandin D2 Elevation in Bald Scalp

animal_models.description: Raises skin prostaglandin D2 genetically, the manipulation of this node.
animal_models.name: K14-Ptgs2 transgenic mouse (skin-targeted prostaglandin overproduction)

evidence.reference_title: Prostaglandin D2 inhibits hair growth and is elevated in bald scalp of men with androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: We show that prostaglandin D(2) synthase (PTGDS) is elevated at the mRNA and protein levels in bald scalp compared to haired scalp of men with AGA.

evidence.reference_title: Prostaglandin D2 inhibits hair growth and is elevated in bald scalp of men with androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: Hair growth inhibition requires the PGD(2) receptor G protein (heterotrimeric guanine nucleotide)-coupled receptor 44 (GPR44), but not the PGD(2) receptor 1 (PTGDR).

nodes.description: The disease is patterned because the follicle's androgen machinery is patterned. Frontal and vertex follicles of affected men and women carry more androgen receptor and more type 1 and type 2 5-alpha-reductase than their own occipital follicles, which instead carry more aromatase; cultured dermal papilla cells from balding scalp bind more androgen than those from non-balding scalp; and dermal papilla cells from occipital scalp show little androgen receptor at all. This is the cellular fact that makes occipital hair spare itself, makes transplanted occipital follicles keep growing in a bald frontal recipient site, and gives the female presentation its milder course, since female frontal follicles carry about 40 percent less receptor and several-fold less 5-alpha-reductase than male ones.
nodes.id: Regional Androgen Sensitivity of Frontal and Vertex Scalp Follicles

animal_models.description: Reproduces the frontal-versus-occipital and adult-versus-juvenile dependence of the dermal papilla's androgen response.
animal_models.name: Stump-tailed macaque spontaneous androgen-dependent frontal balding

cell_types: scalp hair follicle dermal papilla cell

evidence.reference_title: Different levels of 5alpha-reductase type I and II, aromatase, and androgen receptor in hair follicles of women and men with androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: Findings revealed that both women and men have higher levels of receptors and 5alpha-reductase type I and II in frontal hair follices than in occipital follicles, whereas higher levels of aromatase were found in their occipital follicles.

evidence.reference_title: Different levels of 5alpha-reductase type I and II, aromatase, and androgen receptor in hair follicles of women and men with androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: Androgen receptor content in female frontal hair follicles was approximately 40% lower than in male frontal hair follicle.

evidence.reference_title: Balding hair follicle dermal papilla cells contain higher levels of androgen receptors than those from non-balding scalp.
evidence.snippet: Balding cells contained significantly (P < 0.01) greater levels of androgen receptors (Bmax = 0.06 +/- 0.01 fmol/10(4) cells (mean +/- S.E.M.)) than those from non-balding scalp (0.04 +/- 0.001).

evidence.reference_title: Interaction between dermal papilla cells and follicular epithelial cells in vitro: effect of androgen.
evidence.snippet: Androgen receptors were detected in the dermal papilla cells of beard and axillary hair follicles, but not in those of occipital scalp hair follicles.

nodes.description: The one animal in which pattern baldness arises spontaneously in a form close to the human disease. Frontal scalp follicles regress after puberty as serum testosterone and dihydrotestosterone rise, in both sexes; the inhibitory effect of testosterone on epithelial proliferation appears only with dermal papilla cells from the bald frontal scalp of adults and not with cells from hairy occipital scalp or from prebald juveniles, and is blocked by the androgen receptor antagonist RU 58841. Six months of oral finasteride lowered serum dihydrotestosterone by 60 to 70 percent and increased frontal hair weight and follicle length, and topical RU 58841 regrew frontal hair. It carried much of the preclinical work on 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors and antiandrogens.
nodes.id: Stump-tailed macaque spontaneous androgen-dependent frontal balding

evidence.reference_title: Inhibition of hair growth by testosterone in the presence of dermal papilla cells from the frontal bald scalp of the postpubertal stumptailed macaque.
evidence.snippet: Our animal studies also showed that RU 58841 has a dramatic effect on hair regrowth in the bald frontal scalp of the stumptailed macaque, which may further support our in vitro culture studies showing that antiandrogens can antagonize testosterone-elicited hair growth.

nodes.description: Smoking is associated with both the presence and the progression of pattern hair loss in a meta-analysis of observational studies, and the proposed routes are microvascular injury to the papilla, genotoxic damage, protease imbalance, pro-oxidant induction of perifollicular microinflammation and fibrosis, and a relative hypo-oestrogenic state. All of this is observational and mechanistically inferred; it is curated as an exacerbating factor acting on the inflammatory arm, not as a cause.
nodes.id: Tobacco smoking

evidence.reference_title: Risk factors for androgenetic alopecia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
evidence.snippet: Family history (presence: odds ratio [OR] 2.72, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.85–3.99; progression: OR 4.24, 95% CI 2.77–6.49) and smoking (presence: OR 1.46, 95% CI 1.06–2.01; progression: OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.29–1.99) were significantly associated with both presence and progression of AGA.

evidence.reference_title: Association between smoking and hair loss: another opportunity for health education against smoking?
evidence.snippet: Smoke-induced premature skin ageing has attracted the attention of the medical community, while only recently an observational study has indicated a significant relationship between smoking and baldness.

nodes.id: WNT10A

evidence.reference_title: Androgenetic alopecia: identification of four genetic risk loci and evidence for the contribution of WNT signaling to its etiology.
evidence.snippet: Expression studies in human hair follicle tissue suggest that WNT10A has a functional role in AGA etiology.

nodes.description: The follicular epithelium receives a growth-inhibitory rather than a growth-promoting signal. Dickkopf-1 from the papilla antagonizes canonical Wnt signalling and induces apoptosis of outer root sheath keratinocytes; androgen-treated dermal papilla cells from patients show reduced beta-catenin and activated GSK-3beta and lose the ability to induce hair keratin expression in follicle stem cells, which Wnt activation restores. The consequence in patients is specific: bald scalp retains its KRT15-high bulge stem cells but has lost the CD200-rich and CD34-positive progenitor populations that arise from them, so the defect is in conversion of stem cell to progenitor rather than in the stem cell itself. That is why the follicle is miniaturized rather than destroyed, and why the disease is in principle reversible.
nodes.id: Wnt/Beta-Catenin Inhibition and Impaired Progenitor Conversion in Follicular Epithelium

cell_types: hair follicle bulge keratinocyte stem and progenitor cells

evidence.reference_title: Hair follicle stem cell differentiation is inhibited through cross-talk between Wnt/β-catenin and androgen signalling in dermal papilla cells from patients with androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: Androgen treatment revealed a significant decrease in the cytoplasmic/total β-catenin protein ratio and upregulation of the activity of glycogen synthase kinase-3β in DPC, indicative of canonical Wnt pathway inhibition.

evidence.reference_title: Hair follicle stem cell differentiation is inhibited through cross-talk between Wnt/β-catenin and androgen signalling in dermal papilla cells from patients with androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.snippet: Wnt signalling activation restored the ability of androgen-treated DPC to induce differentiation.

evidence.reference_title: Dihydrotestosterone-inducible dickkopf 1 from balding dermal papilla cells causes apoptosis in follicular keratinocytes.
evidence.snippet: Also, recombinant human DKK-1 inhibited the growth of ORS cells and triggered apoptotic cell death.

evidence.reference_title: Bald scalp in men with androgenetic alopecia retains hair follicle stem cells but lacks CD200-rich and CD34-positive hair follicle progenitor cells.
evidence.snippet: These KRT15(hi) stem cells were maintained in bald scalp samples.

evidence.reference_title: Bald scalp in men with androgenetic alopecia retains hair follicle stem cells but lacks CD200-rich and CD34-positive hair follicle progenitor cells.
evidence.snippet: These findings support the notion that a defect in conversion of hair follicle stem cells to progenitor cells plays a role in the pathogenesis of AGA.

evidence.reference_title: Characterization and isolation of stem cell-enriched human hair follicle bulge cells.
evidence.snippet: Positive markers for bulge cells included CD200, PHLDA1, follistatin, and frizzled homolog 1, while CD24, CD34, CD71, and CD146 were preferentially expressed by non-bulge keratinocytes.
